criterion_notes.c1: Although the Ahmedabad Slum Networking Project (SNP) delivered household water supply and underground sewerage, the survey sampled exclusively communities that had already benefited from physical slum upgrading (registered CBOs of at least three years) and examines post-delivery resident programme satisfaction and complaining behaviour rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 because it examines participatory governance, CBO institutional activity, NGO-CBO partnership relations (d_ngo, active3, ngo_evl2), and CBO contact with municipal agencies (amc_com, amccntct) for post-project redress. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because its empirical exposures are post-upgrading community meeting attendance, NGO networking, and informal service-assistance contact in participatory project delivery rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, official discretion, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure). SNP's collective neighbourhood application and universal resident contribution requirements are mentioned only as invariant programme background on PDF Page 7 and are not empirically analysed. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence from a January-June 2009 stratified random survey of 300 CBO leaders and members across 38 SNP-registered neighbourhood organisations in Ahmedabad, analysed via descriptive cross-tabulations, logistic regression, and 2SLS models.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports only subjective social-psychological satisfaction and complaining outcomes: closed-ended overall satisfaction with SNP project quality (snp_qual2) and whether respondents volunteered negative comments about poor quality or quantity of water, sewerage, or street lighting in response to a generic open-ended project comment prompt. The authors explicitly distinguish these satisfaction/complaining measures from actual physical service provision and note that complaining or not complaining does not establish actual service levels; no access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (300 individual CBO leaders and members across 38 upgraded slum CBOs in Ahmedabad), study exposures (CBO meeting attendance, NGO relations, municipal/NGO contact), outcomes (overall project satisfaction and service-specific complaints), and study design (cross-sectional stratified survey with logistic regression) are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional stratified random survey analysed with logistic regression (and 2SLS robustness checks)
population_and_sample: 300 CBO leaders and members (out of 320 sampled) from 38 SNP-registered neighbourhood community-based organisations in upgraded slums of Ahmedabad, India (surveyed January-June 2009)
exposure: Sustained CBO participation (meeting attendance in past 6 months), strength of external NGO partnership relations, and frequency of CBO contact with the municipality or sponsoring NGO to improve community conditions
outcome: Overall SNP programme satisfaction (closed-ended 'very satisfactory' rating) and open-ended respondent complaints regarding poor quality or quantity of water, sewerage, and street lighting services
rationale: Excluded (E04 Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 exposure scope). All 38 sampled slum communities had already received SNP physical upgrading as a sampling precondition, and the study measures post-delivery resident programme satisfaction and open-ended complaining behaviour ('social-psychological outcomes' that the authors explicitly distinguish from actual physical service provision and that conflate quality with quantity) rather than household or community water/sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (failing Criteria 1 and 4). In addition, while the study passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 via participatory governance and CBO-NGO-municipal institutional contact, it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type Criterion 2 reading because its empirical exposures are post-upgrading CBO meeting attendance, NGO partnership ties, and informal service-assistance requests rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (SNP's collective application and contribution rules are mentioned only as unanalysed background).
